growth_story.headline: Iraq's income per person rises and falls with oil and war: it peaked in 2016, then fell back over nine years to about where it stood in 2000.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 2000 growth in income per person averaged 11.4 percent a year, but that mostly reflects recovery from the collapse after the 1990–91 war over Kuwait: income per person fell 64.4 percent in 1991, and sanctions cut oil exports to almost nothing until limited sales resumed under the UN Oil-for-Food program from 1996. From 2001 to 2008 growth averaged 1.3 percent, as the 2003 war cut income per person by 38.5 percent before a 49.1 percent rebound in 2004. From 2009 to 2016 it averaged 3.5 percent; oil output kept growing even through the 2014 oil price crash and the war with ISIS, which the World Bank says hit the non-oil economy hard, and income per person peaked in 2016. Since 2017 growth has averaged -2.1 percent, with the 2020 pandemic and oil price shock, OPEC+ limits on oil output from late 2022 into 2025, and falling oil revenue all weighing on output. By 2025 income per person was 18.8 percent below its 2016 peak and about where it first was in 2000.

threads.title: An economy run on oil
threads.text: Oil makes up almost all of Iraq's exports, most of government revenue and more than half of output, so growth follows oil prices and how much oil Iraq can or may pump. OPEC+ output limits held oil production down from late 2022 and were still in force for most of 2025, and income per person fell in each year from 2023 to 2025.

since_last_year.text: In 2026 the conflict in the Middle East and the disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz cut Iraq's oil output and exports sharply. Output and exports began to recover in June and July after a ceasefire, a partial reopening of flows through Hormuz and the re-routing of some exports through Syria, but the World Bank's October 2026 outlook still expects a deep fall in output for the year. This came after income per person had already fallen 1.7 percent in 2023, 3.6 percent in 2024 and 4.2 percent in 2025.

growth_story.tension: The IMF describes a burst of non-oil growth in 2023, yet income per person in the data fell 1.7 percent that year. The sources offer two reasons the boom does not show: OPEC+ limits held down oil output, which is most of the economy, and the population grows fast, so more output is shared among more people.
